Consequently, upon abandoning the mortal body, such an enlightened soul achieves liberation and eternal communion with the Divine.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.9)

shloka_text: वीतरागभयक्रोधा मन्मया मामुपाश्रिताः। बहवो ज्ञानतपसा पूता मद्भावमागताः।।4.10।।
translation: Freed from attachment, fear, and anger, fully absorbed in Me and taking refuge in Me, many persons in the past, purified by the penance of knowledge, have attained My divine nature.
meaning: The path to God-realization is an empirically proven spiritual highway traversed successfully by countless seekers throughout history. Entering this sanctuary requires freedom from psychological afflictions such as material craving, existential fear, and resentment. By anchoring awareness firmly in God, the devotee surrenders all conditional reliances for divine refuge. The rigorous pursuit of spiritual wisdom acts as a purifying crucible that incinerates latent impressions of ignorance. Thus sanctified, the individual consciousness merges harmoniously into the transcendent nature of the Divine.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.10)

shloka_text: ये यथा मां प्रपद्यन्ते तांस्तथैव भजाम्यहम्। मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः।।4.11।।
translation: In whatever way men surrender unto Me, I reciprocate with them accordingly; for everyone follows My path in all respects, O son of Pritha.
meaning: This verse exemplifies the profound inclusivity and egalitarian nature of divine grace. The Supreme reciprocates with living entities in exact alignment with the purity, intent, and attitude of their approach. Whether approached as a benevolent father, intimate friend, master, or transcendent reality, the Lord manifests accordingly. Even those seeking transient worldly fulfillments through diverse pathways are ultimately seeking aspects of the one Supreme Reality. God remains devoid of favoritism, responding dynamically to each soul's degree of surrender and consciousness.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.11)

shloka_text: काङ्क्षन्तः कर्मणां सिद्धिं यजन्त इह देवताः। क्षिप्रं हि मानुषे लोके सिद्धिर्भवति कर्मजा।।4.12।।
translation: Desiring success in material activities, people worship celestial deities in this world; for in the realm of humans, success born of fruitive action is quickly achieved.
meaning: The majority of mortals are driven by immediate aspirations for wealth, recognition, and tangible mundane outcomes. Consequently, they tend to venerate various celestial administrative powers rather than dedicating themselves to supreme liberation. In this human realm, ritualistic endeavors oriented toward material goals yield swift and visible results. However, such achievements are inherently transient, perishable, and ultimately reinforce the cycle of worldly transmigration. The truly enlightened individual renounces these immediate gratifications to seek the imperishable treasure of spiritual realization.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.12)

shloka_text: चातुर्वर्ण्यं मया सृष्टं गुणकर्मविभागशः। तस्य कर्तारमपि मां विद्ध्यकर्तारमव्ययम्।।4.13।।
translation: The four orders of society were created by Me according to the distinctions of gunas (modes of nature) and karmas (actions); although I am their creator, know Me to be the changeless non-doer.
meaning: The Lord clarifies that the fourfold social classification is fundamentally based upon psychological qualities and aptitudes, rather than birthright. For the collective harmony of humanity, vocations naturally align with intellect, administration, commerce, and productive service. An individual's temperament corresponds directly to the unique configuration of the three modes of nature: sattva, rajas, and tamas. Although the Divine orchestrates this universal framework of creation, He remains fundamentally untouched by its operations. Standing transcendent and unattached, the Supreme operates as the eternal, non-acting observer of all cosmic phenomena.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.13)

shloka_text: न मां कर्माणि लिम्पन्ति न मे कर्मफले स्पृहा। इति मां योऽभिजानाति कर्मभिर्न स बध्यते।।4.14।।
translation: Actions do not taint Me, nor do I have any longing for the fruits of action; one who comprehends Me in this truth is likewise never bound by karma.
meaning: The Supreme sustains, preserves, and dissolves the cosmos while remaining completely free from self-interest or desire for outcomes. Where there is no egoistic motivation or personal attachment, the binding reactions of actions cannot adhere. When a spiritual practitioner realizes this transcendent principle and mirrors it in daily duty, liberation becomes immediate. Entanglement does not stem from the performance of work itself, but from the illusory sense of doership and selfish craving. By emulating this divine detachment, a person works effortlessly within the world without accumulating karmic baggage.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.14)

shloka_text: एवं ज्ञात्वा कृतं कर्म पूर्वैरपि मुमुक्षुभिः। कुरु कर्मैव तस्मात्त्वं पूर्वैः पूर्वतरं कृतम्।।4.15।।
translation: Knowing this truth, the seekers of liberation in ancient times also performed their prescribed duties. Therefore, you too should perform your duty as was done by the ancients in earlier times.
meaning: Lord Krishna points to historical archetypes such as King Janaka, who attained supreme enlightenment not by fleeing action, but through dedicated duty. Genuine liberation does not demand physical abandonment of societal responsibilities, but the internal cessation of selfish motives. Since generations of enlightened sages have achieved perfection through this attitude, it represents a proven and dependable path. Arjuna is gently cautioned against renouncing his warrior duties under the misguided impression that work is incompatible with spirituality. Following the footsteps of these venerable predecessors ensures both societal harmony and personal spiritual liberation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.15)

shloka_text: किं कर्म किमकर्मेति कवयोऽप्यत्र मोहिताः। तत्ते कर्म प्रवक्ष्यामि यज्ज्ञात्वा मोक्ष्यसेऽशुभात्।।4.16।।
translation: What is action and what is inaction? Even the wise are bewildered in this matter. Therefore, I shall explain to you the nature of action, knowing which you shall be liberated from all misfortune.
meaning: The critical distinction between action and inaction is not determined by external movement, but by the internal state of consciousness. Superficially, physical activity appears as action while sitting quietly resembles inaction, yet this perception is deceptive. Even eminent philosophers and learned scholars often find themselves perplexed regarding which deeds bind and which emancipate. Recognizing this profound ambiguity, the Lord undertakes to reveal the deep metaphysical science underlying human activity. Mastering this insight releases the spiritual practitioner from the pervasive miseries of material transmigration.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.16)

shloka_text: कर्मणो ह्यपि बोद्धव्यं बोद्धव्यं च विकर्मणः। अकर्मणश्च बोद्धव्यं गहना कर्मणो गतिः।।4.17।।
translation: The true nature of action must be understood, the nature of forbidden action must be understood, and the nature of inaction must also be understood; indeed, profound and unfathomable is the path of action.
meaning: The underlying architecture of human karma is exceedingly intricate and transcends simplistic ethical reductions. 'Karma' encompasses ordained, righteous duties performed in harmony with universal cosmic order. 'Vikarma' signifies prohibited, selfish, or malicious acts that precipitate moral decline and spiritual suffering. 'Akarma' refers to transcendent, selfless action devoid of ego, which generates no binding reactions whatsoever. Because the subtle repercussions of intentionality are so profound, discernment of this threefold dynamic demands refined spiritual maturity.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.17)

shloka_text: कर्मण्यकर्म यः पश्येदकर्मणि च कर्म यः। स बुद्धिमान् मनुष्येषु स युक्तः कृत्स्नकर्मकृत्।।4.18।।
translation: One who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is truly wise among humans; such a person is a yogi and the complete performer of all actions.
meaning: This verse presents one of the most paradoxical and illuminating teachings of the entire Bhagavad Gita. Perceiving inaction in action means recognizing that while the body performs duties, the transcendent Self remains utterly unattached and non-acting. Perceiving action in inaction exposes the reality that merely abstaining from physical work while harboring mental desires is still binding activity. The sage who realizes this truth works actively in society yet remains untainted by psychological entanglements. Such an awakened soul is hailed as truly wise, perfectly integrated, and an accomplished practitioner of Yoga.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.18)

shloka_text: यस्य सर्वे समारम्भाः कामसङ्कल्पवर्जिताः। ज्ञानाग्निदग्धकर्माणं तमाहुः पण्डितं बुधाः।।4.19।।
translation: One whose all undertakings are devoid of personal desire and fruitive intent, and whose actions are burnt by the fire of divine knowledge, is called a sage by the wise.
meaning: A true sage is defined not by external academic credentials, but by complete emancipation from egoistic ambition. When actions are initiated without selfish expectations or personal attachments, they cease to construct future karmic destiny. Divine knowledge functions like a transcendent fire that burns the seeds of reaction before they can germinate into future suffering. Such an individual acts solely for the welfare of the world, operating as an unblemished instrument of the cosmic will. The truly enlightened recognize such a selfless laborer as a genuine master of wisdom.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.19)

shloka_text: त्यक्त्वा कर्मफलासङ्गं नित्यतृप्तो निराश्रयः। कर्मण्यभिप्रवृत्तोऽपि नैव किञ्चित्करोति सः।।4.20।।
translation: Having abandoned all attachment to the fruits of action, ever content and dependent on nothing, though fully engaged in work, he practically does nothing at all.
meaning: This verse describes the zenith of spiritual autonomy and unshakeable inner contentment. When an individual ceases to hinge inner fulfillment upon worldly outcomes, perpetual serenity naturally emerges. Such a person is 'nirashraya,' or free from psychological dependence upon changing external circumstances, resting solely in the Divine. Superficially, they may appear vigorously immersed in demanding duties and complex responsibilities. Yet, because the illusion of personal agency and selfish desire has vanished, their soul incurs absolutely no karmic entanglement.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.20)

shloka_text: निराशीर्यतचित्तात्मा त्यक्तसर्वपरिग्रहः। शारीरं केवलं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम्।।4.21।।
translation: Free from expectations, with the mind and lower self perfectly subdued, having relinquished all sense of possessiveness, performing work merely for the sustenance of life, one incurs no sin.
meaning: Authentic renunciation is fundamentally an inward state of consciousness rather than the mere abandonment of physical assets. When a seeker becomes devoid of selfish anticipation, the agitations of mind and sensory impulses naturally subside. Having surrendered the psychology of possessiveness, one utilizes material necessities without clinging to the illusion of ownership. Physical activities are performed simply to maintain biological life, dedicated entirely to selfless service. Operating with such unblemished detachment, the practitioner remains untainted by sinful reactions or guilt.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.21)

shloka_text: यदृच्छालाभसन्तुष्टो द्वन्द्वातीतो विमत्सरः। समः सिद्धावसिद्धौ च कृत्वापि न निबध्यते।।4.22।।
translation: Content with whatever comes naturally without effort, rising above the dualities, free from envy, and equipoised in success and failure, one is never bound even while acting.
meaning: This verse presents the quintessential portrait of an unshakeable and spiritually liberated actor in the drama of life. The practitioner rests contented with whatever comes unbidden through the grace of cosmic order. Ascending beyond psychological dualities like pleasure and pain, honor and disgrace, the mind remains utterly serene. Envy completely evaporates because the awakened soul perceives the divine presence operating equally in all beings. Remaining poised whether worldly endeavors culminate in victory or setback, such an individual remains perpetually free.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.22)

shloka_text: गतसङ्गस्य मुक्तस्य ज्ञानावस्थितचेतसः। यज्ञायाचरतः कर्म समग्रं प्रविलीयते।।4.23।।
translation: For one who is devoid of attachment, liberated, whose mind is firmly established in divine wisdom, and who acts solely for the sake of sacrifice, all karma completely dissolves.
meaning: When an individual's awareness is securely anchored in transcendental wisdom, spiritual emancipation is achieved here and now. The practitioner sheds every trace of possessive clinging and egoic self-interest. Daily activities cease to be secular tasks; they transform into sacred oblations performed solely for cosmic service and divine pleasure. Because no trace of selfish agency remains, actions generate no psychological residues or binding impressions upon the consciousness. All past and present karmic reactions dissolve entirely, like mist evaporating before the morning sun.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.23)

shloka_text: ब्रह्मार्पणं ब्रह्महविर्ब्रह्माग्नौ ब्रह्मणा हुतम्। ब्रह्मैव तेन गन्तव्यं ब्रह्मकर्मसमाधिना।।4.24।।
translation: Brahman is the offering; Brahman is the oblation poured into the fire of Brahman by Brahman; one who is fully absorbed in action as Brahman certainly reaches Brahman alone.
meaning: This profound verse encapsulates the non-dual realization wherein the entirety of existence is recognized as pure Divinity. To the illumined seer, every component of an action is a manifestation of the single Absolute Reality. The instrument of sacrifice, the oblation offered, the fire that consumes it, and the offerer are all perceived as Brahman. When every worldly duty is performed with this unitive absorption, life itself becomes a continuous state of samadhi. Whosoever abides in this constant awareness of divine omnipresence merges irrevocably into the Supreme Consciousness.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.24)

shloka_text: दैवमेवापरे यज्ञं योगिनः पर्युपासते। ब्रह्माग्नावपरे यज्ञं यज्ञेनैवोपजुह्वति।।4.25।।
translation: Some yogis perform sacrifice to celestial deities, while other mystics offer the self as a sacrifice into the fire of the Supreme Brahman through the act of sacrifice itself.
meaning: The Lord broadens the concept of 'yajna' from ritualistic fire sacrifices to diverse dimensions of spiritual disciplines. Beginners often engage in devotional worship and rituals dedicated to celestial energies to cleanse their desires. In contrast, advanced contemplative yogis perform the internal sacrifice of offering their finite individuality into the fire of the Infinite. For such seers, the total absorption of the ego into non-dual Brahman represents the supreme culmination of sacrifice. Hence, authentic yajna evolves from outward performance into radical, inward spiritual self-surrender.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.25)

shloka_text: श्रोत्रादीनीन्द्रियाण्यन्ये संयमाग्निषु जुह्वति। शब्दादीन्विषयानन्य इन्द्रियाग्निषु जुह्वति।।4.26।।
translation: Some offer the sense of hearing and other senses into the fires of self-restraint, while others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound, into the fires of the senses.
meaning: This verse presents two distinct yogic approaches to sensory mastery within the framework of sacred sacrifice. The first path represents strict ascetics who withdraw their senses from sensory allurements, incinerating desire in the fire of self-restraint. The second path describes balanced householders who engage with sense objects without psychological addiction or lustful clinging. By receiving experiences with inner detachment, they transform everyday sensory perceptions into pure, harmless offerings. Both disciplines converge upon the essential goal of transcending sensory slavery to attain spiritual equilibrium.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.26)

shloka_text: सर्वाणीन्द्रियकर्माणि प्राणकर्माणि चापरे। आत्मसंयमयोगाग्नौ जुह्वति ज्ञानदीपिते।।4.27।।
translation: Others offer all the activities of the senses and the functions of the vital life energy into the fire of the yoga of self-control, kindled by wisdom.
meaning: This discipline describes the pinnacle of Raja Yoga, wherein the practitioner focuses the entirety of personal energy inward. All outgoing activities of the sensory organs and the autonomic functions of the vital breath are deliberately stabilized. This self-control is not a forced, unnatural suppression, but an enlightened mastery ignited by spiritual wisdom. As mental fluctuations cease and the mind becomes anchored in pure consciousness, personal turbulence dissolves completely. In this sublime state of meditative absorption, the seeker experiences profound tranquility and transcendental bliss.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.27)

shloka_text: द्रव्ययज्ञास्तपोयज्ञा योगयज्ञास्तथापरे। स्वाध्यायज्ञानयज्ञाश्च यतयः संशितव्रताः।।4.28।।
translation: Observing austere vows, some ascetics practice sacrifice through material wealth, some through penance, others through the practice of eightfold yoga, and still others through sacred study and the pursuit of knowledge.
meaning: The Lord acknowledges the rich diversity of spiritual inclinations, showing that multiple disciplines lead to the identical divine summit. Those performing wealth-sacrifice offer material resources for societal welfare with absolute unselfishness. Practitioners of austerity-sacrifice voluntarily undertake disciplinary purifications to master the body and instinctual urges. Yoga-sacrifice involves the systematic practice of breath regulation, inward withdrawal, and mental concentration. Lastly, seekers of wisdom engage in scriptural reflection and self-inquiry, offering ignorance into the quest for ultimate truth.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.28)

shloka_text: अपाने जुह्वति प्राण प्राणेऽपानं तथाऽपरे। प्राणापानगती रुद्ध्वा प्राणायामपरायणाः।।4.29।।
translation: Likewise, other practitioners offer the outgoing breath into the incoming breath, and the incoming into the outgoing, and stopping the movement of both, remain devoted to breath control.
meaning: This verse describes the esoteric science of Pranayama, portraying breath regulation as a sacred sacrifice. The incoming breath (apana) and outgoing breath (prana) are consciously harmonized and unified through focused awareness. By mastering inhalation, exhalation, and breathless retention (kumbhaka), the restless fluctuations of mental energy are stilled. Because the life force and mental waves are intimately entwined, governing the respiration tranquilizes consciousness. This internal sacrifice purifies the nervous system and creates an optimal interior environment for divine communion.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.29)

shloka_text: अपरे नियताहाराः प्राणान्प्राणेषु जुह्वति। सर्वेऽप्येते यज्ञविदो यज्ञक्षपितकल्मषाः।।4.30।।
translation: Others, restricting their food intake, offer the life energies into the life energies themselves. All these knowers of sacrifice have their impurities cleansed through their performance of sacrifice.
meaning: Regulated and wholesome diet plays an indispensable role in maintaining spiritual vitality and clarity. By moderating their sustenance, practitioners prevent bodily lethargy and avoid dissipating vital energies in digestive strain. The conserved pranic force is directed upward, offering vital energies into the focused stream of life energy itself. The Lord emphasizes that irrespective of the specific methodology employed, authentic sacrifice burns away latent psychic impurities. Cleansed of moral and mental imperfections, all these knowers of sacrifice qualify for spiritual enlightenment.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.30)

shloka_text: यज्ञशिष्टामृतभुजो यान्ति ब्रह्म सनातनम्। नायं लोकोऽस्त्ययज्ञस्य कुतो़ऽन्यः कुरुसत्तम।।4.31।।
translation: Those who partake of the nectarean remnants of sacrifice attain the eternal Brahman. For one who performs no sacrifice, neither this world nor the next can offer happiness, O best of the Kurus.
meaning: The sacred remnants of selfless action are regarded as divine nectar that purifies human existence. One who serves society and honors the Divine prior to indulging individual desires leads an elevated and blessed life. Savoring the nectar of sacrifice, such an individual progressively ascends to the realization of the eternal Absolute. Conversely, a completely self-absorbed individual who recognizes no obligation to others finds no authentic peace even in this world. Devoid of the spirit of dedication, higher spiritual realms remain utterly inaccessible to the selfish soul.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.31)

shloka_text: एवं बहुविधा यज्ञा वितता ब्रह्मणो मुखे। कर्मजान्विद्धि तान्सर्वानेवं ज्ञात्वा विमोक्ष्यसे।।4.32।।
translation: Thus, various kinds of sacrifices are spread out in the words of the Vedas; know them all to be born of action, and knowing this truth, you shall be liberated.
meaning: The Vedic scriptures enumerate an extensive spectrum of sacrifices tailored to diverse temperaments and human inclinations. Every sacrifice, whether physical, mental, or intellectual, fundamentally originates within the realm of human action and nature. The immortal Soul, however, remains forever transcendental, luminous, and distinct from worldly mechanics. Realizing that all activities are simply interactions of nature's modes frees the seeker from false egoistic identification. By mastering this metaphysical discrimination, the practitioner breaks the bonds of material conditioned existence.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.32)

shloka_text: श्रेयान्द्रव्यमयाद्यज्ञाज्ज्ञानयज्ञः परन्तप। सर्वं कर्माखिलं पार्थ ज्ञाने परिसमाप्यते।।4.33।।
translation: Superior is the sacrifice of knowledge to any sacrifice of material possessions, O scorcher of foes; for all action in its entirety culminates in divine wisdom, O son of Pritha.
meaning: The Lord proclaims that the internal sacrifice of wisdom infinitely surpasses any ritual performed with material resources. While material offerings can bring societal welfare and temporary merit, they remain limited by physical constraints. Conversely, the sacrifice of knowledge systematically dissolves the root cause of suffering, which is spiritual ignorance. Every ritualistic deed and philanthropic effort is ultimately intended to prepare the mind for the dawn of pure wisdom. When transcendental illumination is achieved, all purposeful human actions reach their ultimate fulfillment and conclusion.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.33)

shloka_text: तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया। उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः।।4.34।।
translation: Learn that Truth by approaching a spiritual master, by humble inquiry, and by rendering service; those who have realized the Truth will impart that knowledge unto you.
meaning: This classic verse delineates the three essential conditions for acquiring authentic spiritual wisdom from an enlightened master. The first requirement is 'pranipat,' representing humble prostration and the complete surrender of intellectual pride. The second is 'pariprashna,' which denotes sincere, reflective inquiry directed toward truth rather than argumentative debate. The third is 'seva,' or selfless service, which purifies the disciple's vessel and fosters genuine spiritual receptivity. Only self-realized seers who have directly perceived the Ultimate Reality possess the capacity to awaken that dormant vision in a receptive seeker.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.34)

shloka_text: यज्ज्ञात्वा न पुनर्मोहमेवं यास्यसि पाण्डव। येन भूतान्यशेषेण द्रक्ष्यस्यात्मन्यथो मयि।।4.35।।
translation: Having realized this knowledge, O Pandava, you shall never again fall into such delusion; by this wisdom you shall perceive all living beings within your own self, and then in Me.
meaning: The definitive hallmark of genuine spiritual illumination is the permanent eradication of existential delusion and sorrow. Just as brilliant sunlight dispels lingering darkness, the dawn of Self-realization annihilates psychological confusion forever. This transcendent vision expands consciousness so vastly that the seeker perceives all diverse beings existing within the unified Self. Furthermore, the awakened person realizes that the Self and all creation reside eternally within the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Attaining this unitive vision permanently dissolves all hatred, fear, and artificial senses of separation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.35)

shloka_text: अपि चेदसि पापेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः पापकृत्तमः। सर्वं ज्ञानप्लवेनैव वृजिनं सन्तरिष्यसि।।4.36।।
translation: Even if you were the most sinful of all sinners, you would cross over the entire ocean of sin by the boat of transcendental knowledge alone.
meaning: This verse offers monumental hope and boundless redemption to even the most morally compromised individual. Sin is fundamentally an outcome of spiritual amnesia and ignorance, never the intrinsic nature of the immortal soul. Transcendental knowledge possesses such immense transformative power that it nullifies lifetimes of accrued guilt and karmic consequences. Just as a sturdy vessel effortlessly navigates a turbulent and treacherous ocean, the raft of divine wisdom carries the soul beyond the sea of sins. Taking refuge in spiritual truth guarantees that inner resurrection is achievable for every sincere seeker.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.36)

shloka_text: यथैधांसि समिद्धोऽग्निर्भस्मसात्कुरुतेऽर्जुन। ज्ञानाग्निः सर्वकर्माणि भस्मसात्कुरुते तथा।।4.37।।
translation: As a blazing fire turns firewood to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions and their reactions to ashes.
meaning: The Lord presents a vivid and illuminating metaphor to illustrate the absolute purifying potency of spiritual realization. Regardless of the volume or weight of timber thrown into a roaring fire, the flames inexorably consume it into harmless ash. Similarly, when the blazing fire of divine wisdom awakens within human consciousness, it obliterates accumulated mountains of past karmic impressions. Once the root illusion of individual doership is incinerated, deeds lose their capacity to generate binding future consequences. Thus, the enlightened soul engages in outward actions with complete internal purity and freedom.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.37)

shloka_text: न हि ज्ञानेन सदृशं पवित्रमिह विद्यते। तत्स्वयं योगसंसिद्धः कालेनात्मनि विन्दति।।4.38।।
translation: In this world, there is certainly nothing as purifying as divine knowledge; one who has perfected oneself through the practice of Yoga finds this wisdom within the Self in due course of time.
meaning: Within the entire cosmos, there exists no purifying agent comparable to the supreme nectar of transcendental knowledge. Worldly ablutions, external pilgrimages, and formal rituals merely cleanse the physical periphery, whereas wisdom purifies the core of consciousness. This realization cannot be procured externally through transactional means; it blossoms spontaneously from within as the fruit of steadfast Yoga. As the mind becomes gradually stabilized and purged of selfish cravings, this inner light illuminates the heart in the maturity of time. Therefore, the spiritual aspirant must cultivate patient perseverance while steadfastly walking the path of duty.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.38)

shloka_text: श्रद्धावाँल्लभते ज्ञानं तत्परः संयतेन्द्रियः। ज्ञानं लब्ध्वा परां शान्तिमचिरेणाधिगच्छति।।4.39।।
translation: A person endowed with faith, fully dedicated to it, and possessing mastery over the senses, attains divine knowledge; having attained knowledge, one quickly achieves supreme peace.
meaning: Lord Krishna presents three indispensable prerequisites for securing transformative spiritual illumination: firm faith, steadfast dedication, and sensory restraint. Faith (shraddha) is not uncritical credulity, but deep intuitive conviction in the teachings of the scriptures and enlightened masters. Steadfast dedication implies relentless devotion to the spiritual quest, undeterred by transient distractions. Mastery of the senses prevents the precious dissipation of mental energy, focusing awareness directly inward toward the Divine. When these virtues converge, the seeker quickly attains that supreme, unshakeable peace which surpasses all worldly understanding.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.39)

shloka_text: अज्ञश्चाश्रद्दधानश्च संशयात्मा विनश्यति। नायं लोकोऽस्ति न परो न सुखं संशयात्मनः।।4.40।।
translation: The ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish; for the skeptical mind, there is neither this world, nor the world beyond, nor any happiness.
meaning: Doubt is a corrosive psychological poison that undermines human resolve, clarity, and spiritual integrity. One who lacks basic spiritual discernment and rejects faith inevitably drifts into confusion and despair. A chronically cynical mind, paralyzed by perpetual suspicion, cannot commit wholeheartedly to any noble endeavor. Such a skeptical individual forfeits the joy of worldly relationships while simultaneously remaining barred from transcendent spiritual realms. Eradicating destructive inner doubt is therefore essential for achieving both worldly well-being and eternal liberation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.40)

shloka_text: योगसंन्यस्तकर्माणं ज्ञानसंछिन्नसंशयम्। आत्मवन्तं न कर्माणि निबध्नन्ति धनञ्जय।।4.41।।
translation: One who has renounced all actions through the practice of Yoga, whose doubts have been torn to shreds by wisdom, and who is securely anchored in the Self, is not bound by karma, O conqueror of wealth.
meaning: This verse portrays the supreme synergy of dedicated Karma Yoga and illuminating Jnana Yoga. When an individual surrenders the fruits of every activity unto the Divine, work itself becomes spiritual renunciation. By severing the roots of existential hesitation with the sword of wisdom, the intellect becomes profoundly unified. Grounding identity unshakeably in the immortal Self, the practitioner rises above physical conditioning. Such an anchored soul may perform monumental worldly actions, yet remains eternally unencumbered by their karmic repercussions.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.41)

shloka_text: तस्मादज्ञानसंभूतं हृत्स्थं ज्ञानासिनाऽऽत्मनः। छित्त्वैनं संशयं योगमातिष्ठोत्तिष्ठ भारत।।4.42।।
translation: Therefore, sever with the sword of knowledge this doubt residing in your heart, born of ignorance; establish yourself in Karma Yoga and arise, O descendant of Bharata!
meaning: In this resounding conclusion to the fourth chapter, Lord Krishna delivers a clarion call to decisive spiritual action. The paralyzing hesitation afflicting Arjuna's heart is identified as an offspring of fundamental spiritual ignorance. Such dark inner delusions cannot be resolved through sentimentality, but must be severed by the luminous blade of Self-knowledge. Arjuna is commanded to take firm refuge in detached Karma Yoga rather than evading his moral duties as a warrior. This stirring exhortation summons every spiritual seeker to vanquish inner skepticism and bravely confront the battlefield of life.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (4.42)

shloka_text: अर्जुन उवाच संन्यासं कर्मणां कृष्ण पुनर्योगं च शंससि। यच्छ्रेय एतयोरेकं तन्मे ब्रूहि सुनिश्िचतम्।।5.1।।
translation: Arjuna said: O Krishna, at one moment You praise the renunciation of actions, and then again You commend the path of selfless action. Tell me conclusively which of these two is definitely more beneficial for me.
meaning: At the threshold of the fifth chapter, Arjuna articulates the natural perplexity experienced by sincere spiritual practitioners. The Lord had previously praised the intellectual renunciation of action while simultaneously urging intense engagement on the battlefield. Perceiving an apparent contradiction between the monastic withdrawal of sannyasa and the outward engagement of karma yoga, Arjuna seeks clarity. He requests a definitive, unambiguous prescription regarding which pathway guarantees the highest spiritual welfare. This pivotal question sets the stage for resolving the ancient debate between outward renunciation and enlightened worldly action.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.1)

shloka_text: श्री भगवानुवाच संन्यासः कर्मयोगश्च निःश्रेयसकरावुभौ। तयोस्तु कर्मसंन्यासात्कर्मयोगो विशिष्यते।।5.2।।
translation: The Supreme Lord said: Renunciation of action (Sannyasa) and action in devotion (Karma Yoga) both lead to the supreme good. But of the two, Karma Yoga is superior to the renunciation of actions.
meaning: Lord Krishna states in this verse that both renunciation of action (Sannyasa) and action in devotion (Karma Yoga) lead to the ultimate good. He clarifies that although both paths lead to liberation, Karma Yoga is superior to the mere renunciation of actions. In Karma Yoga, an individual performs their duties without attachment to the results, which leads to quicker purification of the mind. This path is particularly suitable for householders and those who wish to progress spiritually while living in the world. Karma Yoga emphasizes the renunciation of the fruits of action, not the actions themselves, making it a practical approach.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.2)

shloka_text: ज्ञेयः स नित्यसंन्यासी यो न द्वेष्टि न काङ्क्षति। निर्द्वन्द्वो हि महाबाहो सुखं बन्धात्प्रमुच्यते।।5.3।।
translation: O mighty-armed one, know him to be a perpetual renunciant who neither hates nor desires anything. Such a person, free from dualities, is easily liberated from bondage.
meaning: Lord Krishna here defines a true renunciant, whose identity is determined not by external abandonment but by internal disposition. Such a person neither hates anyone nor desires anything, understanding that all dualities arise from Maya. They rise above pairs of opposites like pleasure and pain, gain and loss, keeping their mind calm and steady. Thus, they are easily liberated from the bondage of actions and attain supreme peace. This internal detachment is the foundation of true renunciation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.3)

shloka_text: सांख्ययोगौ पृथग्बालाः प्रवदन्ति न पण्डिताः। एकमप्यास्थितः सम्यगुभयोर्विन्दते फलम्।।5.4।।
translation: Only the ignorant speak of Sankhya (renunciation of actions) and Karma Yoga as different, not the learned. For one who is truly established in either of them attains the fruit of both.
meaning: In this verse, Lord Krishna clarifies the unity between Jnana Yoga (Sankhya) and Karma Yoga. He states that only the ignorant consider these two paths as separate, whereas the wise understand them as two different means leading to the same goal. If a person sincerely follows even one of these paths completely, they attain the fruit of both. This implies that whether through knowledge or through selfless action, the ultimate goal is self-realization and liberation. Therefore, there is no real difference between these two paths, only a difference in approach.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.4)

shloka_text: यत्सांख्यैः प्राप्यते स्थानं तद्योगैरपि गम्यते। एकं सांख्यं च योगं च यः पश्यति स पश्यति।।5.5।।
translation: The state that is attained by followers of Sankhya (Jnana Yoga) is also attained by followers of Karma Yoga. Therefore, one who sees Sankhya and Karma Yoga as one truly sees.
meaning: Lord Krishna reiterates that the ultimate goal of Jnana Yoga and Karma Yoga is the same. The supreme state attained through Sankhya (Jnana Yoga) can also be achieved through Karma Yoga. This indicates that both paths lead to the same spiritual destination, even if their processes differ. One who perceives these two as different facets of the same truth is truly a seer of reality. This understanding frees an individual from the narrow-mindedness of considering one path superior and grants them a broader spiritual perspective.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.5)

shloka_text: संन्यासस्तु महाबाहो दुःखमाप्तुमयोगतः। योगयुक्तो मुनिर्ब्रह्म नचिरेणाधिगच्छति।।5.6।।
translation: O mighty-armed one, renunciation (of actions) is difficult to attain without Karma Yoga. A sage engaged in Karma Yoga quickly attains Brahman.
meaning: Lord Krishna further clarifies the importance of Karma Yoga in this verse. He states that merely renouncing actions, or taking sannyasa, is extremely difficult without the practice of Karma Yoga. The reason is that without purification of the mind and control over the senses, mere external renunciation does not lead to true peace. Conversely, a sage who is engaged in Karma Yoga quickly attains Brahman by controlling their mind and senses. Karma Yoga teaches an individual the art of performing actions without attachment, thereby easily progressing towards liberation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.6)

shloka_text: योगयुक्तो विशुद्धात्मा विजितात्मा जितेन्द्रियः। सर्वभूतात्मभूतात्मा कुर्वन्नपि न लिप्यते।।5.7।।
translation: One who is united in consciousness with God, whose intellect is purified, who has conquered the mind and senses, and who sees the Soul of all souls in every living being, is never entangled, even while performing actions.
meaning: This verse describes the qualities of an ideal Karma Yogi, who stands at the pinnacle of spiritual advancement. Such a Yogi remains situated in God, meaning their consciousness is always connected to the Supreme Being. Their soul is purified, mind is controlled, and senses are fully subdued, making them unaffected by external temptations. Most importantly, they perceive the same Soul in all beings, fostering a sense of equanimity. In this state, even while performing actions, they are not entangled by their results, as their actions are devoid of attachment.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.7)

shloka_text: नैव किंचित्करोमीति युक्तो मन्येत तत्त्ववित्। पश्यन् श्रृणवन्स्पृशञ्जिघ्रन्नश्नन्गच्छन्स्वपन् श्वसन्।।5.8।।
translation: A knower of truth, steadfast in Karma Yoga, even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing, thinks, 'I do nothing at all,' for he knows that it is the senses that are engaged with their objects.
meaning: This verse describes the internal state of a Karma Yogi who is a knower of truth. They consider all their physical and mental activities as the natural engagement of the senses with their objects. Even while seeing, hearing, touching, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing, they do not consider themselves the doer. They understand that all these actions are being performed by the modes of nature, and the soul is beyond all of them. Thus, even while performing actions, they remain free from the bondage of karma, as they have no ego of doership. This profound understanding grants them ultimate peace and liberation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.8)

shloka_text: प्रलपन्विसृजन्गृह्णन्नुन्मिषन्निमिषन्नपि। इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेषु वर्तन्त इति धारयन्।।5.9।।
translation: Even while talking, giving up, accepting, opening and closing the eyes, (the knower of truth) considers that the senses are engaged with their objects.
meaning: This verse illustrates the continuous awareness of a knower of truth that they are not the doer. They consider actions like speaking, giving up, accepting, and opening-closing eyes as the natural engagement of the senses. This profound understanding keeps them detached from the fruits of actions, as they do not consider themselves the master of these activities. They know that the soul is beyond all these material actions and is merely a witness. Thus, even while living in the world, they remain free from the bondage of actions.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.9)

shloka_text: ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः। लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा।।5.10।।
translation: One who performs actions, dedicating them to Brahman and abandoning attachment, is not affected by sin, just as a lotus leaf remains untouched by water.
meaning: This verse presents the essence of Karma Yoga with a beautiful analogy. One who performs all actions, dedicating them to Brahman (the Supreme Being) and abandoning attachment to their results, remains untouched by sin. Just as a lotus leaf remains unwetted by water even while being in it, similarly, such a Karma Yogi remains free from the bondage of actions even while living in the world. This renunciation of attachment protects an individual from the good and bad consequences of actions. This state is the result of internal purity and equanimity, leading to liberation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.10)

shloka_text: कायेन मनसा बुद्ध्या केवलैरिन्द्रियैरपि। योगिनः कर्म कुर्वन्ति सङ्गं त्यक्त्वाऽऽत्मशुद्धये।।5.11।।
translation: Karma Yogis perform actions with their body, mind, intellect, and even with their senses, abandoning attachment, for the purification of the self.
meaning: This verse describes the method and purpose of a Karma Yogi's actions. Karma Yogis renounce attachment in all actions performed by their body, mind, intellect, and senses. Their primary objective is self-purification, not the attainment of any personal gain. They understand that attachment to the fruits of actions is the cause of bondage, and therefore they abandon it. Thus, all their actions become as sacred as a sacrifice and lead them towards spiritual progress. This selfless action paves the way for self-realization.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.11)

shloka_text: युक्तः कर्मफलं त्यक्त्वा शान्तिमाप्नोति नैष्ठिकीम्। अयुक्तः कामकारेण फले सक्तो निबध्यते।।5.12।।
translation: One who is united in consciousness with God, abandoning the results of actions, attains everlasting peace. One who is not united with God in consciousness, impelled by desires, becomes entangled by attachment to the results.
meaning: This verse compares the outcomes of a Karma Yogi and a non-Yogi. A Karma Yogi, united with the Supreme, attains supreme and everlasting peace by renouncing the fruits of actions. Their peace is permanent because it does not depend on external outcomes. Conversely, a person who is not united with God, driven by their desires, becomes attached to the results of actions. This attachment binds them to the cycle of worldly existence, preventing them from ever achieving true peace. Therefore, the renunciation of attachment is the path to liberation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.12)

shloka_text: सर्वकर्माणि मनसा संन्यस्यास्ते सुखं वशी। नवद्वारे पुरे देही नैव कुर्वन्न कारयन्।।5.13।।
translation: The embodied being, the self-controlled one, happily resides in the city of nine gates (the body), having mentally renounced all actions, neither doing anything nor causing anything to be done.
meaning: This verse describes the state of a self-realized person who, though residing in the body, remains detached from it. They consider their body as a city with nine gates, in which they reside as the embodied soul. Such a self-realized person mentally renounces all actions, meaning they do not consider themselves the doer of actions. They neither perform any action themselves nor cause others to do so, as they know that all activities are performed by the modes of nature. Thus, they live happily and peacefully, free from the bondage of actions.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.13)

shloka_text: न कर्तृत्वं न कर्माणि लोकस्य सृजति प्रभुः। न कर्मफलसंयोगं स्वभावस्तु प्रवर्तते।।5.14।।
translation: The Lord (God) neither creates the sense of doership for people, nor actions, nor the connection with the fruits of actions. It is one's own nature (Prakriti) that acts.
meaning: In this verse, Lord Krishna clarifies that the Supreme Being neither inspires anyone to act nor connects them with the fruits of actions. He neither creates the sense of doership nor originates actions. In reality, all of this is governed by the modes of nature, referred to as 'svabhava' (one's own nature). The living entity acts according to its nature and experiences the results. The Supreme Being is merely a witness; He does not interfere in the actions of any living entity but maintains His neutrality.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.14)

shloka_text: नादत्ते कस्यचित्पापं न चैव सुकृतं विभुः। अज्ञानेनावृतं ज्ञानं तेन मुह्यन्ति जन्तवः।।5.15।।
translation: The omnipresent God neither accepts anyone's sin nor their virtuous deeds. Knowledge is covered by ignorance, and by that, living entities are deluded.
meaning: Lord Krishna further clarifies the detachment of the Supreme Being in this verse. He states that the Supreme Lord neither accepts the results of anyone's sinful actions nor their virtuous deeds. God is beyond the fruits of all actions and remains neutral. Whatever good or bad actions a living entity performs, they alone must experience the consequences. It is ignorance that covers the true knowledge of the living entity, due to which they become deluded in the world, considering themselves the doer. Because of this ignorance, living entities remain trapped in the cycle of birth and death.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.15)

shloka_text: ज्ञानेन तु तदज्ञानं येषां नाशितमात्मनः। तेषामादित्यवज्ज्ञानं प्रकाशयति तत्परम्।।5.16।।
translation: But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by divine knowledge, their knowledge, like the sun, illumines that Supreme Entity.
meaning: This verse describes the effect of the destruction of ignorance and the dawn of self-knowledge. For those individuals whose ignorance is dispelled by the light of self-knowledge, the ultimate truth becomes clear. Their knowledge shines like the sun, dispelling all darkness and revealing the Supreme Entity (Brahman) to them. This knowledge is not merely intellectual understanding but a profound spiritual realization that frees an individual from the illusion of Maya. In this state, the living entity recognizes its true identity and experiences its unity with the Supreme Being.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.16)

shloka_text: तद्बुद्धयस्तदात्मानस्तन्निष्ठास्तत्परायणाः। गच्छन्त्यपुनरावृत्तिं ज्ञाननिर्धूतकल्मषाः।।5.17।।
translation: Those whose intellect is directed toward God, whose heart is solely absorbed in God, who have firm faith in God, and who strive after God as the supreme goal and refuge, such persons, whose sins have been dispelled by knowledge, attain the state from which there is no return (liberation).
meaning: This verse describes the state of devotees who are completely surrendered to the Supreme Being. Their intellect, mind, faith, and ultimate goal are all centered solely on God. Such individuals, through knowledge, wash away all their sins and ignorance, thereby becoming purified. As a result of this purification, they attain that supreme state from which they do not have to take birth again in this world. This state of 'no return' is called liberation, which is complete freedom from the cycle of birth and death. This is the outcome of unwavering devotion and knowledge of the Supreme Being.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.17)

shloka_text: विद्याविनयसंपन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि। शुनि चैव श्वपाके च पण्डिताः समदर्शिनः।।5.18।।
translation: The learned ones see with equal vision a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a dog-eater (outcaste).
meaning: This verse describes the characteristic of a true knower, who possesses a sense of equanimity. Such a wise person sees the same soul in a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste. They do not give importance to external differences, as they know that the same fragment of the Supreme Soul resides in all bodies. This equal vision is the symbol of true knowledge, which fills them with love and compassion for all beings. This state frees an individual from ego and discrimination.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.18)

shloka_text: इहैव तैर्जितः सर्गो येषां साम्ये स्थितं मनः। निर्दोषं हि समं ब्रह्म तस्माद्ब्रह्मणि ते स्थिताः।।5.19।।
translation: Those whose minds are situated in equanimity have conquered creation in this very life. Because Brahman is flawless and equal, they are therefore situated in Brahman.
meaning: This verse highlights the importance of equanimity and its fruit. Those individuals whose minds remain situated in equanimity in all circumstances conquer the cycle of birth and death in this very life. The reason for this is that Brahman itself is flawless and equal, and when the mind attains equanimity, it becomes one with Brahman. In this state, a person experiences themselves as situated in Brahman and remains unaffected by the dualities of the world. This sense of equanimity is the direct path to liberation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.19)

shloka_text: न प्रहृष्येत्प्रियं प्राप्य नोद्विजेत्प्राप्य चाप्रियम्। स्थिरबुद्धिरसम्मूढो ब्रह्मविद्ब्रह्मणि स्थितः।।5.20।।
translation: One who neither rejoices upon obtaining the pleasant nor becomes disturbed upon attaining the unpleasant, whose intellect is steady, who is undeluded, and who knows Brahman, is situated in Brahman.
meaning: This verse describes the characteristic of a knower of Brahman, who is beyond dualities like pleasure and pain, pleasant and unpleasant. Such a person neither rejoices upon obtaining a pleasant object nor becomes disturbed upon attaining an unpleasant one, because their intellect is steady. They are not deluded in any situation and always remain situated in self-knowledge. This equanimous and steady intellect is the proof of their being established in Brahman. This state keeps an individual unaffected by the ups and downs of the world and grants them inner peace.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.20)

shloka_text: बाह्यस्पर्शेष्वसक्तात्मा विन्दत्यात्मनि यत्सुखम्। स ब्रह्मयोगयुक्तात्मा सुखमक्षयमश्नुते।।5.21।।
translation: One whose self is unattached to external sense pleasures finds happiness within the self. Such a person, whose soul is united with God through Yoga, experiences unlimited happiness.
meaning: This verse describes the superiority of inner happiness. A person whose self is not attached to external sense objects experiences true happiness within themselves. This happiness is eternal and self-reliant, unlike fleeting and changeable external pleasures. Such a person, who unites their soul with the Supreme Being through Brahma Yoga, attains imperishable (never-ending) happiness. This inner bliss is the foundation of liberation, which does not depend on external circumstances.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.21)

shloka_text: ये हि संस्पर्शजा भोगा दुःखयोनय एव ते। आद्यन्तवन्तः कौन्तेय न तेषु रमते बुधः।।5.22।।
translation: O son of Kunti, indeed, the pleasures born of contact with the sense objects are verily sources of misery. They have a beginning and an end, therefore the wise person does not delight in them.
meaning: Lord Krishna here highlights the transient nature and sorrowful essence of external sense pleasures. He explains to Arjuna that all enjoyments arising from contact with sense objects are momentary and ultimately lead to misery. These pleasures have a beginning and an end, meaning they are not permanent. A wise person knows this truth and therefore does not become attached to such fleeting pleasures. They understand that true and lasting happiness lies only in inner self-knowledge, not in external objects.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.22)

shloka_text: शक्नोतीहैव यः सोढुं प्राक्शरीरविमोक्षणात्। कामक्रोधोद्भवं वेगं स युक्तः स सुखी नरः।।5.23।।
translation: One who is able to withstand the impulses arising from desire and anger in this very body, before giving it up, is a Yogi and a happy person.
meaning: This verse describes the importance of self-control and its fruits. Lord Krishna states that one who is able to withstand the intense impulses arising from desire and anger in this mortal body, before giving it up, is a true Yogi. Such a person alone experiences real happiness in this world, as they are the master of their senses and mind. Conquering desire and anger is a crucial milestone in spiritual progress, which provides an individual with inner peace and stability.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.23)

shloka_text: योऽन्तःसुखोऽन्तरारामस्तथान्तर्ज्योतिरेव यः। स योगी ब्रह्मनिर्वाणं ब्रह्मभूतोऽधिगच्छति।।5.24।।
translation: One who is happy within the self, who enjoys within the self, and who is illumined by the inner light, that Yogi, being united with the Lord, attains liberation from material existence.
meaning: This verse describes the state of a Yogi who has attained complete self-realization. Such a Yogi does not seek happiness in external objects but experiences joy and peace within themselves. They revel in their inner self and are illumined by the light of inner knowledge. When a Yogi attains this state, they become 'Brahmabhuta', meaning they experience oneness with Brahman. In this state, they achieve Brahma-nirvana, which is complete liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.24)

shloka_text: लभन्ते ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृषयः क्षीणकल्मषाः। छिन्नद्वैधा यतात्मानः सर्वभूतहिते रताः।।5.25।।
translation: Those holy persons whose sins have been purged, whose doubts have been annihilated, whose minds are disciplined, and who rejoice in the welfare of all living entities, attain liberation from material existence.
meaning: This verse describes the qualities of sages who attain Brahma-nirvana. Such sages are those whose sinful actions have been destroyed and whose doubts of the mind have been completely dispelled. They have fully controlled their minds and are constantly engaged in the welfare of all living entities. Their selfless service and internal purity liberate them from the bondage of birth and death, leading them to attain supreme peace and liberation. This state is a confluence of knowledge, devotion, and service.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.25)

shloka_text: कामक्रोधवियुक्तानां यतीनां यतचेतसाम्। अभितो ब्रह्मनिर्वाणं वर्तते विदितात्मनाम्।।5.26।।
translation: For those saintly persons who are liberated from desires and anger, whose minds are subdued, and who are self-realized, liberation from material existence exists on all sides.
meaning: This verse describes the state of self-realized ascetics who are completely free from desire and anger. They have fully subdued their minds and have realized the true nature of their soul. For such individuals, Brahma-nirvana (liberation) is accessible from all sides, as they are already internally liberated. Their consciousness always remains situated in Brahman, due to which the bondage of the world cannot affect them. This state is a symbol of ultimate peace and freedom.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.26)

shloka_text: स्पर्शान्कृत्वा बहिर्बाह्यांश्चक्षुश्चैवान्तरे भ्रुवोः। प्राणापानौ समौ कृत्वा नासाभ्यन्तरचारिणौ।।5.27।।
translation: Keeping external sense objects outside, fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, and making the incoming and outgoing breaths (Prana and Apana) equal within the nostrils (the Yogi should meditate).
meaning: This verse describes the preliminary physical and mental preparations for Dhyana Yoga. The Yogi should detach themselves from external sense objects to calm the mind. Fixing the gaze between the eyebrows helps to enhance concentration. Making the incoming and outgoing breaths (Prana and Apana) equal within the nostrils is an important part of Pranayama, which stabilizes the mind. These actions are fundamental for the depth of meditation, leading to inner peace. This practice frees the mind from external distractions.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.27)

shloka_text: यतेन्द्रियमनोबुद्धिर्मुनिर्मोक्षपरायणः। विगतेच्छाभयक्रोधो यः सदा मुक्त एव सः।।5.28।।
translation: One who has controlled the senses, mind, and intellect, who is dedicated to liberation, and who is free from desire, fear, and anger, that sage is always liberated.
meaning: This verse describes the state of a sage who has attained complete self-control. One who has fully subdued their senses, mind, and intellect remains unaffected by external influences. Such a sage considers liberation as their ultimate goal, and all their endeavors are directed towards it. They are completely free from all impurities like desire, fear, and anger, which grants them inner peace. In this state, even while living in the world, they are always liberated, as their mind is situated in the Supreme Being.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.28)

shloka_text: भोक्तारं यज्ञतपसां सर्वलोकमहेश्वरम्। सुहृदं सर्वभूतानां ज्ञात्वा मां शान्तिमृच्छति।।5.29।।
translation: Having realized Me (Lord Krishna) as the enjoyer of all sacrifices and austerities, the Supreme Lord of all worlds, and the selfless friend of all living beings, one attains supreme peace.
meaning: This verse describes the ultimate fruit of divine knowledge. When a person realizes Lord Krishna as the sole enjoyer of all sacrifices and austerities, the Supreme Lord of all worlds, and the selfless friend of all living beings, they attain supreme peace. This knowledge destroys an individual's ego and makes them experience oneness with the Supreme Being. With this understanding, all doubts are dispelled, and they rise above the dualities of the world. This divine knowledge is the source of true and lasting peace.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (5.29)

shloka_text: श्री भगवानुवाच अनाश्रितः कर्मफलं कार्यं कर्म करोति यः। स संन्यासी च योगी च न निरग्निर्न चाक्रियः।।6.1।।
translation: The Supreme Lord said: One who performs obligatory work without desiring the results of actions is a Sannyasi and a Yogi, not merely one who has given up the sacrificial fire or renounced all activities.
meaning: Lord Krishna defines a true Sannyasi and Yogi here. He clarifies that real renunciation or Yoga lies not in external abandonment but in internal detachment. One who performs their duties without desiring the fruits of actions is a true Sannyasi and Yogi. A person who merely gives up the sacrificial fire or renounces all activities is not a Sannyasi if attachment persists in their mind. This verse re-establishes the importance of Karma Yoga, where the renunciation of attachment to the fruits of actions, not the actions themselves, is crucial.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.1)

shloka_text: यं संन्यासमिति प्राहुर्योगं तं विद्धि पाण्डव। न ह्यसंन्यस्तसङ्कल्पो योगी भवति कश्चन।।6.2।।
translation: O son of Pandu, know that which is called Sannyasa to be Yoga, for no one can become a Yogi without renouncing desires (for the fruits of actions).
meaning: Lord Krishna explains to Arjuna that Sannyasa and Yoga are essentially the same, as both are fundamentally based on the renunciation of desires. Sannyasa does not merely mean external renunciation, but the mental abandonment of all desires and intentions. Similarly, Yoga is the process of freeing the mind from desires by controlling it. Until an individual renounces the desires and intentions of their mind, they cannot become a true Yogi. This verse emphasizes the importance of internal detachment and control over desires, which are essential for progress on the spiritual path.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.2)

shloka_text: आरुरुक्षोर्मुनेर्योगं कर्म कारणमुच्यते। योगारूढस्य तस्यैव शमः कारणमुच्यते।।6.3।।
translation: For a sage who wishes to ascend to Yoga, action (selfless action) is said to be the means. For one who has ascended to Yoga, tranquility (of mind) is said to be the means.
meaning: This verse describes two stages of the path of Yoga. In the initial stage, when a sage desires to ascend to Yoga, selfless action is the means for them. Through Karma Yoga, they purify their mind and renounce attachments. When they have ascended to Yoga, meaning they have attained a higher state of Yoga, then tranquility (peace of mind and control of senses) becomes the means for them. In this state, external actions are no longer necessary; rather, internal stability and meditation become paramount.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.3)

shloka_text: यदा हि नेन्द्रियार्थेषु न कर्मस्वनुषज्जते। सर्वसङ्कल्पसंन्यासी योगारूढस्तदोच्यते।।6.4।।
translation: When a person is neither attached to sense objects nor to actions, and has renounced all desires for the fruits of actions, then they are said to have ascended to Yoga.
meaning: This verse describes the state when a seeker is called 'Yoga-arudha' (one who has ascended to Yoga). A person is said to be Yoga-arudha when they have no attachment whatsoever to sense objects or to their actions. This means they are completely free from external temptations and the desire for the fruits of actions. They renounce all desires, meaning there are no cravings or plans in their mind. This internal detachment and non-attachment are symbols of the higher state of Yoga, where the mind becomes completely calm and steady.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.4)

shloka_text: उद्धरेदात्मनाऽऽत्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत्। आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः।।6.5।।
translation: One should uplift oneself by one's own self, and not degrade oneself. For the mind is indeed one's friend, and the mind is also one's enemy.
meaning: This verse emphasizes the importance of self-effort and self-reliance. Lord Krishna states that every individual should uplift themselves by their own efforts and never degrade themselves. Our mind can be our greatest friend or our greatest enemy. If the mind is controlled and directed in the right direction, it paves the way for liberation. However, if the mind is uncontrolled and attached to worldly objects, it becomes the cause of bondage and suffering. Therefore, control over the mind is the key to spiritual progress.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.5)

shloka_text: बन्धुरात्माऽऽत्मनस्तस्य येनात्मैवात्मना जितः। अनात्मनस्तु शत्रुत्वे वर्तेतात्मैव शत्रुवत्।।6.6।।
translation: For one who has conquered their mind, the mind is their friend. But for one who has not conquered their mind, the mind acts like an enemy.
meaning: This verse elaborates on the previous one, clarifying the dual nature of the mind. For a person who has conquered their mind by withdrawing it from the senses and their objects, and has achieved self-control, their mind becomes their best friend. Such a mind helps them progress on the spiritual path and provides inner peace. Conversely, for one who has not conquered their mind, that very mind acts like an enemy, entangling them in worldly objects and leading to suffering and bondage. Therefore, conquering the mind is true freedom.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.6)

shloka_text: जितात्मनः प्रशान्तस्य परमात्मा समाहितः। शीतोष्णसुखदुःखेषु तथा मानापमानयोः।।6.7।।
translation: For one who has conquered their mind and is peaceful, the Supreme Soul (God) remains steadfast in cold and heat, happiness and distress, as well as in honor and dishonor.
meaning: This verse describes the elevated spiritual state of a person who has conquered their mind and is peaceful. For such an individual, the Supreme Soul (God) always remains steadfast and absorbed, meaning they remain situated in God. They remain unaffected by dualities like cold and heat, happiness and distress, honor and dishonor. Their inner peace is so profound that external circumstances cannot disturb them. This state is the ultimate example of equanimity, where a person remains balanced in all situations and experiences their unity with the Supreme Being.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.7)

shloka_text: ज्ञानविज्ञानतृप्तात्मा कूटस्थो विजितेन्द्रियः। युक्त इत्युच्यते योगी समलोष्टाश्मकाञ्चनः।।6.8।।
translation: One whose soul is fully satisfied with knowledge and realized wisdom, who is undisturbed, who has conquered the senses, and who regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, such a Yogi is said to be 'Yukta' (united with the Supreme).
meaning: This verse describes the qualities of a perfected Yogi. Such a Yogi is fully satisfied with knowledge (scriptural understanding) and realized wisdom (experiential knowledge), which keeps their soul content. They are undisturbed, meaning they remain unmoving and steady in all circumstances, and they have completely conquered their senses. For them, a clod of earth, a stone, and gold all hold equal value, as they know the transient nature of material objects. Such a person is called 'Yukta', meaning they are fully united with the Supreme Being.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.8)

shloka_text: सुहृन्मित्रार्युदासीनमध्यस्थद्वेष्यबन्धुषु। साधुष्वपि च पापेषु समबुद्धिर्विशिष्यते।।6.9।।
translation: One who has an impartial intellect towards well-wishers, friends, enemies, neutral persons, mediators, the envious, relatives, the pious, and even sinners, is distinguished (superior).
meaning: This verse illustrates the pinnacle of equanimity, which is the hallmark of an advanced Yogi. Such a Yogi maintains an impartial intellect towards well-wishers, friends, enemies, neutral persons, mediators, the envious, relatives, the pious, and even sinners. They harbor no attachment or aversion towards anyone, as they perceive the same soul in all. This equal vision frees them from all forms of discrimination and grants them supreme peace. This state signifies the highest level of spiritual development, where an individual holds equal love and compassion for all beings.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.9)

shloka_text: योगी युञ्जीत सततमात्मानं रहसि स्थितः। एकाकी यतचित्तात्मा निराशीरपरिग्रहः।।6.10।।
translation: A Yogi should constantly engage the self in meditation, remaining in seclusion, alone, with a controlled mind and body, free from desires, and free from possessions for enjoyment.
meaning: This verse describes the necessary conditions and qualities for the practice of Dhyana Yoga. A Yogi should reside alone in a secluded place to avoid external distractions. They must keep their mind and body completely under control to achieve stability in meditation. They should be free from any kind of hope or desire and should not accumulate possessions for enjoyment. With these qualities, the Yogi should constantly engage their self in the Supreme Being to attain self-realization.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.10)

shloka_text: शुचौ देशे प्रतिष्ठाप्य स्थिरमासनमात्मनः। नात्युच्छ्रितं नातिनीचं चैलाजिनकुशोत्तरम्।।6.11।।
translation: In a clean place, one should establish a firm seat for oneself, which is neither too high nor too low, and on which a cloth, a deerskin, and Kusha grass are spread one over the other.
meaning: This verse provides a detailed description of the appropriate seat and place for meditation. A Yogi should choose a clean and sacred place where they can meditate peacefully. They should establish a firm seat for themselves, which is neither too high nor too low, to maintain bodily stability. On this seat, Kusha grass, deerskin, and a cloth should be spread one over the other, to protect them from external influences. This proper seat and place are extremely important for the depth and concentration of meditation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.11)

shloka_text: तत्रैकाग्रं मनः कृत्वा यतचित्तेन्द्रियक्रियः। उपविश्यासने युञ्ज्याद्योगमात्मविशुद्धये।।6.12।।
translation: Seated on that seat, making the mind one-pointed, controlling the activities of the mind and senses, the Yogi should strive to practice Yoga for the purification of the self.
meaning: This verse describes the actual process of Dhyana Yoga. The Yogi should sit on their designated seat and make their mind one-pointed, so as not to be distracted by external thoughts. They must control all activities of their mind and senses, so they do not hinder meditation. Thus, they practice Yoga with the aim of self-purification, meaning their goal is solely the attainment of inner purity and self-knowledge. This concentration and self-control are the keys to the success of Yoga.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.12)

shloka_text: समं कायशिरोग्रीवं धारयन्नचलं स्थिरः। संप्रेक्ष्य नासिकाग्रं स्वं दिशश्चानवलोकयन्।।6.13।।
translation: Holding the body, head, and neck straight and unmoving, remaining steady, gazing at the tip of one's own nose, and not looking in other directions (the Yogi should meditate).
meaning: This verse provides detailed instructions for the physical posture during meditation. The Yogi should hold their body, head, and neck straight and steady, keeping the spine erect. They should sit unmoving and stable, so that bodily movements do not distract the mind. Their gaze should be fixed on the tip of their nose, which helps in concentrating the mind and preventing distraction by external sights. Not looking in other directions is also essential for mental concentration.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.13)

shloka_text: प्रशान्तात्मा विगतभीर्ब्रह्मचारिव्रते स्थितः। मनः संयम्य मच्चित्तो युक्त आसीत मत्परः।।6.14।।
translation: With a serene mind, fearless, situated in the vow of celibacy, having controlled the mind, meditating on Me (Shree Krishna), and having Me as the supreme goal, the Yogi should sit.
meaning: This verse describes the internal qualities and goal of a Dhyana Yogi. The Yogi should have a serene mind and be fearless, enabling them to meditate without hindrance. They should be situated in the vow of celibacy, which is essential for energy and concentration. By completely controlling their mind, they should fix their consciousness on Lord Krishna. Considering God as their supreme goal, the Yogi should sit in meditation to achieve oneness with the Supreme Being. This is a beautiful confluence of devotion and Yoga.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.14)

shloka_text: युञ्जन्नेवं सदाऽऽत्मानं योगी नियतमानसः। शान्तिं निर्वाणपरमां मत्संस्थामधिगच्छति।।6.15।।
translation: Thus, a Yogi with a disciplined mind, constantly keeping the mind absorbed in God, attains the supreme peace of liberation from material bondage, which abides in Me.
meaning: This verse describes the ultimate fruit of practicing Dhyana Yoga. A Yogi who, by disciplining their mind, constantly keeps their soul absorbed in the Supreme Being, attains supreme peace. This peace is not ordinary peace, but 'Nirvana-paramam', meaning the supreme peace of complete liberation from the cycle of birth and death. Lord Krishna states that this supreme peace abides in Him, implying that it is attained by becoming one with the Supreme Being. This state signifies the end of all suffering and the attainment of eternal bliss.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.15)

shloka_text: नात्यश्नतस्तु योगोऽस्ति न चैकान्तमनश्नतः। न चातिस्वप्नशीलस्य जाग्रतो नैव चार्जुन।।6.16।।
translation: O Arjuna, this Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who abstains from eating altogether. It is not for one who sleeps too much, nor for one who remains awake all the time.
meaning: This verse emphasizes the importance of balance in Yoga practice. Lord Krishna explains to Arjuna that the path of Yoga is not one of extremism. It is neither for those who eat too much nor for those who fast completely. Similarly, it is neither for those who sleep excessively nor for those who remain awake all the time. To achieve success in Yoga, moderation and balance are essential in all aspects of life. Any kind of excess destabilizes the mind and body, thereby hindering meditation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.16)

shloka_text: युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु। युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दुःखहा।।6.17।।
translation: For one whose eating and recreation are moderate, whose efforts in actions are balanced, and whose sleep and wakefulness are regulated, their Yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrows.
meaning: This verse describes the moderation necessary for the destruction of sorrows through Yoga. Lord Krishna states that one whose eating and recreation are moderate maintains physical and mental health. One whose efforts in actions are balanced remains free from attachment and stress. One whose sleep and wakefulness are also regulated remains energetic and focused. The Yoga of such a disciplined person becomes the destroyer of all sorrows and grants them supreme peace.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.17)

shloka_text: यदा विनियतं चित्तमात्मन्येवावतिष्ठते। निःस्पृहः सर्वकामेभ्यो युक्त इत्युच्यते तदा।।6.18।।
translation: When the fully controlled mind remains steadfast in the self, and one becomes free from all cravings for sense objects, then one is said to be 'Yukta' (situated in perfect Yoga).
meaning: This verse defines a 'Yukta' Yogi. A person is called 'Yukta' when their fully controlled mind becomes steadfast only in the self. In this state, they become completely free from all kinds of desires and cravings for sense objects. No worldly desire remains for them, as they have attained inner bliss. This internal stability and freedom from desires are the pinnacle of Yoga, where an individual becomes one with the Supreme Being.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.18)

shloka_text: यथा दीपो निवातस्थो नेङ्गते सोपमा स्मृता। योगिनो यतचित्तस्य युञ्जतो योगमात्मनः।।6.19।।
translation: As a lamp placed in a windless place does not flicker, that analogy is considered for a Yogi whose mind is disciplined and who is steadily practicing Yoga on the Supreme Self.
meaning: This verse clarifies the state of a Yogi with a concentrated mind through a beautiful analogy. Just as a lamp placed in a windless place burns steadily without flickering, similarly, the mind of a Yogi practicing Yoga for self-realization remains steady and concentrated. External distractions or internal desires have no effect on their mind. This stability is a symbol of the depth and success of meditation, which helps them achieve oneness with the Supreme Being.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.19)

shloka_text: यत्रोपरमते चित्तं निरुद्धं योगसेवया। यत्र चैवात्मनाऽऽत्मानं पश्यन्नात्मनि तुष्यति।।6.20।।
translation: When the mind, restrained by the practice of Yoga, becomes still, and when the Yogi, beholding the soul through the purified mind, is satisfied in the self.
meaning: This verse describes the advanced state of Yoga where the mind becomes completely still. When all mental modifications are restrained through continuous practice of Yoga, the mind attains supreme peace. In this state, the Yogi realizes their own soul through their purified intellect and mind. They do not seek happiness in external objects but experience complete satisfaction within their own self. This inner bliss and self-realization are the ultimate goals of Yoga.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.20)

shloka_text: सुखमात्यन्तिकं यत्तद्बुद्धिग्राह्यमतीन्द्रियम्। वेत्ति यत्र न चैवायं स्थितश्चलति तत्त्वतः।।6.21।।
translation: In which state the Yogi knows that limitless happiness, which is grasped by the intellect and transcends the senses, and being situated in which, they never deviate from the Eternal Truth.
meaning: This verse describes the supreme happiness attained in the ultimate state of Yoga. This happiness transcends the senses, meaning it cannot be experienced through the senses, but is grasped only by the purified intellect. The Yogi knows this transcendental happiness, which is eternal and boundless. Situated in this state, they never deviate from the Eternal Truth, meaning they never forget their true identity and their unity with the Supreme Being. This stability is the foundation of liberation.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.21)

shloka_text: यं लब्ध्वा चापरं लाभं मन्यते नाधिकं ततः। यस्मिन्स्थितो न दुःखेन गुरुणापि विचाल्यते।।6.22।।
translation: Having gained which, one considers no other gain greater than that, and being situated in which, one is not shaken even by the greatest sorrow.
meaning: This verse highlights the significance of the ultimate achievement attained through Yoga. When a Yogi achieves this inner bliss and self-realization, they consider it superior to any other worldly gain. For them, no worldly pleasure or wealth equals this spiritual benefit. Situated in this state, they are not shaken even by the greatest sorrow or calamity, because their inner peace and stability are unwavering. This supreme state frees an individual from all kinds of fear and anxiety.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.22)

shloka_text: तं विद्याद् दुःखसंयोगवियोगं योगसंज्ञितम्। स निश्चयेन योक्तव्यो योगोऽनिर्विण्णचेतसा।।6.23।।
translation: Know that which severs the connection with misery as Yoga. This Yoga should be practiced with determination and an undeviating mind.
meaning: This verse defines Yoga not merely as physical postures, but as the profound state of liberation from all forms of suffering. True Yoga is the complete severance of the soul's entanglement with the transient miseries of material existence. Lord Krishna emphasizes the critical importance of unwavering determination and a mind free from despondency in pursuing this path. The practitioner must approach this spiritual discipline with resolute conviction, never allowing doubt or weariness to deter their progress. This steadfastness ensures that the seeker remains focused on achieving the ultimate union with the Divine, transcending all worldly afflictions.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.23)

shloka_text: सङ्कल्पप्रभवान्कामांस्त्यक्त्वा सर्वानशेषतः। मनसैवेन्द्रियग्रामं विनियम्य समन्ततः।।6.24।।
translation: Completely abandoning all desires born of mental resolve, and restraining the multitude of senses from all sides by the mind alone.
meaning: A yogi must completely abandon all desires that arise from mental resolve. It is essential to restrain the multitude of senses from all sides by the mind alone. This practice helps to withdraw the mind from external objects and lead it towards inner peace. Without establishing control over the senses, progress on the path of yoga is impossible. Thus, the practitioner purifies their consciousness and moves towards self-realization.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.24)

shloka_text: शनैः शनैरुपरमेद् बुद्ध्या धृतिगृहीतया। आत्मसंस्थं मनः कृत्वा न किञ्चिदपि चिन्तयेत्।।6.25।।
translation: Gradually, one should attain tranquility by the intellect held with firm resolve. Fixing the mind in the Self, one should not think of anything else.
meaning: The practitioner should gradually quiet the mind with an intellect endowed with patience and firm resolve. Fixing the mind in the Supreme Self, one should not contemplate anything else. This state represents the pinnacle of concentration and inner peace. Only through continuous practice can the mind's restlessness be controlled. Thus, the yogi completely calms their consciousness and becomes established in their true Self.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.25)

shloka_text: यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम्। ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत्।।6.26।।
translation: Whenever and wherever the restless and unsteady mind wanders, one should restrain it from there and bring it back under the control of the Self.
meaning: The mind is inherently restless and unsteady, constantly wandering among various objects. Wherever this mind may roam, the practitioner must withdraw it from there. One should repeatedly and diligently fix it upon the Supreme Self. This continuous practice is the only way to bring the mind under control. Thus, by concentrating the mind, one can advance towards self-realization.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.26)

shloka_text: प्रशान्तमनसं ह्येनं योगिनं सुखमुत्तमम्। उपैति शान्तरजसं ब्रह्मभूतमकल्मषम्।।6.27।।
translation: Indeed, the supreme bliss comes to that yogi whose mind is perfectly peaceful, whose passions are subdued, who is free from sin, and who has become one with Brahman.
meaning: The yogi whose mind becomes perfectly peaceful attains supreme bliss. Their passions, born of the quality of rajas, are subdued, freeing them from worldly desires. Such a yogi achieves the state of Brahma-bhūta, where they experience themselves as one with Brahman. They become free from all sins, established in pure consciousness. This state is one of self-realization and ultimate beatitude.
title: Daily Gita Reflection (6.27)
